items.title: Identity Theft Protection Act — notice of security breach
items.citation: MCL 445.72 (Identity Theft Protection Act, Act 452 of 2004, as amended)
items.applies_to_vendor: MCL 445.72(2): 'a person or agency that maintains a database that includes data that the person or agency does not own or license that discovers a breach of the security of the database shall provide a notice to the owner or licensor of the information of the security breach.' This is the vendor/service-provider duty — LOVELEEDAY, as the entity that maintains but does not own client data, must notify the client (data owner/licensor), not the data subjects directly.
key_obligations: A person/agency that owns or licenses data must notify each affected MI resident whose unencrypted personal information was accessed and acquired, unless the breach is determined not likely to cause substantial loss/injury or identity theft (MCL 445.72(1), (3)).
A person/agency that maintains data it does not own must notify the owner/licensor of the breach (MCL 445.72(2)) — this is the vendor duty.
Notice must be given without unreasonable delay, subject to a law-enforcement or scope-investigation delay exception (MCL 445.72(4)).
If notifying more than 1,000 MI residents, must also notify nationwide consumer reporting agencies without unreasonable delay (MCL 445.72(8)).
Entities already compliant with GLBA or HIPAA breach-notice rules are deemed compliant (MCL 445.72(9), (10)).
items.notice_deadline: "without unreasonable delay" (MCL 445.72(4)); vendor-to-owner notice has no separate numeric deadline in the statute.
items.regulator_notice: No statewide-mandatory regulator notice threshold in this section; the Attorney General or a prosecuting attorney may bring an action to recover civil fines for noncompliance (MCL 445.72(13)).
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Defined elsewhere in the Act (MCL 445.63); 445.72 covers unencrypted/unredacted personal information, or encrypted information accessed together with the encryption key.
items.penalties: Fraudulent false notice: misdemeanor, up to 93 days imprisonment and $250/$500/$750 fines for 1st/2nd/3rd+ violations (MCL 445.72(12)). Knowing failure to provide required notice: civil fine up to $250 per failure, aggregate capped at $750,000 per breach event, recoverable by the AG or a prosecuting attorney (MCL 445.72(13)-(14)). Separately, MCL 445.72a (data destruction on removal from database) carries a misdemeanor fine up to $250 per violation.
items.effective_or_amended: 2010 (Act 315, eff. Apr. 1, 2011); original added 2006 (Act 566, eff. July 2, 2007)
items.uncertainty: Fetched full statutory text of MCL 445.72 directly from legislature.mi.gov this session (via curl, since the site's TLS handshake fails Claude's WebFetch tool but is reachable directly) and it supports all fields above. Penalty cross-reference to MCL 445.72a (data-destruction misdemeanor) is separate from the notice-failure penalty in 445.72(13)-(14) itself; both are noted for completeness.

items.title: Student Online Personal Protection Act (SOPPA)
items.applies_to_vendor: Directly binds an 'operator' — defined at MCL 388.1293(e) as 'the operator of an Internet website, online service, online application, or mobile application with actual knowledge that the site, service, or application is used primarily for K–12 school purposes and was designed and marketed for K–12 school purposes.' If LOVELEEDAY builds/operates a K-12-marketed product, it is a regulated operator; if it is a downstream 'service provider' to such an operator, MCL 388.1295(1)(d)(vi) requires the operator's contract with LOVELEEDAY to prohibit LOVELEEDAY from using covered information for any purpose other than the contracted service, prohibit further disclosure, and require reasonable security procedures.
key_obligations: Operator shall not engage in targeted advertising based on information acquired through the K-12 site/service/application (MCL 388.1295(1)(a)).
Operator shall not use information to amass a profile about a student except in furtherance of K-12 school purposes (MCL 388.1295(1)(b)).
Operator shall not sell or rent a student's covered information (MCL 388.1295(1)(c)).

Operator shall not disclose covered information except for the enumerated purposes (school purposes, legal compliance, judicial process, safety/security, requested school/employment purpose, or to a contractually-restricted service provider) (MCL 388.1295(1)(d)).
Operator shall implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of the covered information (MCL 388.1295(2)(a)).
Operator shall delete a student's covered information if the K-12 school or school district requests deletion of information under its control (MCL 388.1295(2)(b)).
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Covered information" (MCL 388.1293(a)) is broad: educational record, e-mail, name, address, phone, discipline records, test results, special-ed data, grades, evaluations, criminal/medical/health records, SSN, biometric information, disabilities, socioeconomic information, food purchases, political affiliation, religious information, text messages, documents, search activity, photos, voice recordings, geolocation.

items.title: Minnesota data warehouses — notice required for certain disclosures
items.applies_to_vendor: Subd. 1(b): a person or business that maintains data it does not own must notify the owner or licensee of the information of any breach of the security of the data immediately following discovery.
key_obligations: Persons/businesses owning or licensing data must disclose breaches to affected MN residents (Subd. 1(a)).
Persons/businesses maintaining data they do not own must notify the owner/licensee immediately following discovery (Subd. 1(b)).

Disclosure must be made in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, consistent with legitimate law-enforcement needs and the measures needed to determine scope, identify affected individuals, and restore system integrity (Subd. 1(a)).
If more than 500 persons must be notified at one time, must also notify all nationwide consumer reporting agencies within 48 hours (Subd. 2).
Any waiver of these requirements is contrary to public policy, void and unenforceable (Subd. 3).
items.notice_deadline: "in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay"; consumer-reporting-agency notice "within 48 hours" when >500 persons affected at one time.
items.regulator_notice: No separate state-regulator notice threshold specified in this section; the Attorney General enforces the section under Minn. Stat. § 8.31 (Subd. 6).
items.penalties: No fixed statutory dollar penalty in 325E.61 itself; enforced by the Attorney General under the general consumer-protection enforcement authority of Minn. Stat. § 8.31.

items.title: Minnesota Government Data Practices Act — educational data / technology providers (Student Data Privacy Act, 2022)
items.applies_to_vendor: Binds a "technology provider" — an entity that contracts with a public educational institution to supply school-issued devices and that creates, receives, or maintains educational data under that contract. If LOVELEEDAY supplies devices/software to a Minnesota school client under such a contract, it is directly regulated and its contract with the school must include the required safeguards.
key_obligations: Technology providers may not sell, share, or disseminate educational data except as authorized by statute or valid contract delegation, and may not use it for any commercial purpose including marketing/advertising to a student or parent.

Government entities and technology providers may not electronically access location-tracking, audio/visual recording, or monitor student interactions (keystrokes, web-browsing activity) with a school-issued device, subject to narrow exceptions (educational purpose, legal warrant, stolen-device recovery, safety threat, legal compliance, federal funding programs) (subd. 14(a)).
School contracts with technology providers must require "appropriate security safeguards" and restrict employee access to those whose official duties require it.
Technology providers must destroy or return all educational data created, received, or maintained under the agreement within 90 days after contract expiration.
Schools must give parents/students direct notice within 30 days of the start of each school year identifying which curriculum/testing providers access student data.
items.notice_deadline: Data destruction/return: within 90 days of contract expiration. Annual parent/student notice: within 30 days of the start of each school year.
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Educational data" is government data as defined in the broader Minnesota Government Data Practices Act (ch. 13); the technology-provider-specific subdivisions were added in 2022.
items.penalties: Violations of the data-practices provisions are enforceable under Minn. Stat. §§ 13.08 (civil remedies) and 13.09 (penalties); exact dollar figures are set in those cross-referenced sections, not in 13.32 itself.
items.effective_or_amended: 2022 (technology-provider subdivisions 13-14 added); other subdivisions amended through 2025.
items.uncertainty: Fetched directly from revisor.mn.gov this session. Did not independently open the cross-referenced §§ 13.08/13.09 penalty text this session, so exact penalty dollar amounts are not quoted (left as a cross-reference rather than a guessed number).

items.title: Minnesota Consumer Data Privacy Act (MCDPA)
items.applies_to_vendor: Directly regulates "processors" (§ 325M.13): a processor must adhere to the controller's instructions and assist the controller in meeting its obligations. LOVELEEDAY, processing client personal data on the client's behalf, is a processor under this framework whenever the client is a covered controller.
key_obligations: Processor must respond to/support consumer-rights requests through appropriate technical and organizational measures.
Processor must support the controller's data-security and breach-notification compliance.
Processing must be governed by a binding written contract specifying processing instructions, data types, and retention terms.
Processor must ensure personnel are subject to confidentiality obligations.
Processor may engage a subcontractor only with the controller's approval, under a binding written agreement imposing equivalent obligations.
Processor must implement technical and organizational security measures.
Processor must delete or return personal data on contract completion, unless retention is legally required.
Processor must give the controller access to information needed to demonstrate compliance and permit assessments.
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Controller" = the person who determines the purposes and means of processing; "processor" = a person who processes personal data on behalf of a controller (definitions section).
items.penalties: Attorney General enforces via civil action under Minn. Stat. § 8.31; civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation. No private right of action for consumers.
items.effective_or_amended: Effective July 31, 2025 (extended compliance to July 31, 2029 for postsecondary institutions regulated by the MN Office of Higher Education).
items.uncertainty: Fetched directly from revisor.mn.gov this session; content reflects a WebFetch summary of the chapter rather than a subsection-by-subsection manual read, so exact subsection numbers within 325M.13 for each processor duty were not individually cited.

items.title: Persons conducting business in Mississippi required to provide notice of a breach of security involving personal information; enforcement
items.applies_to_vendor: A person who conducts business in Mississippi and maintains computerized data that includes personal information the person does not own or license shall notify the owner or licensee of the information of any breach of the security of the data as soon as practicable following its discovery, if the personal information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired by an unauthorized person for fraudulent purposes.
key_obligations: Vendor/third-party maintaining data it does not own must notify the owner/licensee as soon as practicable following discovery (where acquisition was, or is reasonably believed to have been, for fraudulent purposes).

Disclosure must be made without unreasonable delay, subject to the time needed to complete an investigation to determine the nature/scope of the incident, identify affected individuals, or restore reasonable data-system integrity (subsections (4)-(5)).
Failure to comply constitutes an unfair trade practice, enforced by the Attorney General.
The statute does not create a private right of action.
items.notice_deadline: "as soon as practicable" following discovery; general disclosure "without unreasonable delay".
items.penalties: Enforced as an unfair trade practice by the Mississippi Attorney General; no private right of action.

items.title: Student Data Accessibility, Transparency and Accountability Act of 2015 / vendor requirements for K-12 digital and online resources
items.citation: Miss. Code Ann. § 37-15-1 (Student Data Accessibility, Transparency and Accountability Act of 2015, enacted via SB 2777, 2015 Reg. Sess.); Miss. Code Ann. § 37-11-81 (vendor requirements for digital/online K-12 resources)
items.applies_to_vendor: The 2015 Act requires the State Board of Education to adopt rules implementing a data inventory, data-transfer prohibitions, a data security plan, and — most relevant to vendors — requires that contracts governing databases, assessments, or instructional supports that include student or de-identified data and are outsourced to private vendors contain express provisions safeguarding privacy and security, with penalties for vendor noncompliance. Separately, § 37-11-81 conditions a school's ability to offer a vendor's digital/online K-12 resource on the vendor meeting statutory safety-policy and technology-protection-measure requirements, with defined 'noncompliance by providers' consequences.
key_obligations: State Board of Education must maintain a data inventory and develop data-use policies (2015 Act).
Transfer of certain student data is prohibited except under defined exceptions (2015 Act).
State must maintain a data security plan and comply with related laws/policies (2015 Act).

Contracts with private vendors for databases/assessments/instructional supports involving student or de-identified data must include express privacy/security safeguards and noncompliance penalties (2015 Act).

A vendor providing a digital or online K-12 resource must meet statutory requirements before a school/district/state agency may offer that resource to students; noncompliance by the provider has defined consequences (§ 37-11-81).
items.penalties: The 2015 Act requires vendor contracts to include penalty provisions for noncompliance (contractual, not a separate statutory fine schedule identified this session); § 37-11-81 defines consequences for provider noncompliance but the exact text of those consequences was not independently fetched this session.
items.effective_or_amended: 2015 (Student Data Accessibility, Transparency and Accountability Act, enacted via SB 2777)

items.title: Missouri notice of breach of security of data — definitions, procedure
items.applies_to_vendor: Any person that maintains or possesses personal information on behalf of another business, and that does not own or license the information, must notify the owner or licensee of the information of any breach of security immediately following discovery, if the personal information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, accessed and acquired by an unauthorized person.
key_obligations: A person/business that owns or licenses personal information must notify affected Missouri consumers without unreasonable delay.
A third party maintaining personal information it does not own must notify the owner/licensee immediately following discovery of the breach.
Notice must describe the incident generally, the types of information compromised, and provide consumer-reporting-agency contact information and monitoring advice.
Substitute notice permitted where cost of individual notice would exceed $100,000, affected consumers exceed 150,000, or the entity lacks sufficient contact information.
items.notice_deadline: "without unreasonable delay"; vendor-to-owner notice "immediately following discovery of the breach".
items.penalties: The Attorney General has exclusive authority to bring an action for actual damages for a willful and knowing violation and may seek a civil penalty not to exceed $150,000 per breach. No private right of action.

items.title: Missouri Student Data Accessibility, Transparency, and Accountability Act
items.applies_to_vendor: Contracts between the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education (or a school/district) and a private vendor handling student data must include express provisions that safeguard privacy and security, including provisions prohibiting the vendor from selling student data or using it to further advertising. Exceptions exist only for local service providers accessing FERPA-defined 'directory information.'
key_obligations: Vendor contracts must include express privacy/security safeguard provisions.
Vendors are prohibited from selling student data or using it for advertising purposes.
The Department may not collect/report juvenile court delinquency records, criminal records, student biometric information, political affiliation, or religion.

Institutions must maintain a comprehensive data security plan (access authorization/authentication, privacy compliance, routine audits, breach-notification procedures, data retention/disposition, encryption and staff training).
The Department may not transfer personally identifiable student data except as provided by law and authorized policy.
items.penalties: Civil penalties: up to $1,000 for a first violation; up to $5,000 for a subsequent violation by the same entity involving the same student; up to $10,000 for further violations. Enforced by the Attorney General through investigation and civil action.

items.title: Montana Consumer Data Privacy Act
items.applies_to_vendor: Directly regulates "processors" (§ 30-14-2813, "Data processor -- allowances -- limitations"): processors must adhere to controller instructions and assist the controller in meeting its Act obligations. LOVELEEDAY processing client personal data as a service provider is a processor when its client is a covered controller.
key_obligations: Processor-controller relationship must be governed by a binding contract specifying the nature, purpose, duration and type of data subject to processing, and both parties' rights/obligations.
Processor personnel handling data must be subject to a duty of confidentiality.
Processor must delete or return all personal data on controller request, unless legal retention applies.
Processor must assist the controller in meeting security and breach-notification obligations (cross-referencing § 30-14-1704).
Processor must help the controller respond to consumer-rights requests using appropriate technical/organizational measures.
Processor must, on reasonable request, provide information necessary to demonstrate compliance and allow (or arrange an independent qualified assessor for) compliance assessments.
Any subcontractor must be engaged under a written contract imposing the same processor-level obligations.
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Controllers had until January 1, 2025 to support recognized universal opt-out preference signals (§ 30-14-2809).
items.penalties: Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority (§ 30-14-2817); no private right of action. A 30-day statutory cure opportunity exists before an enforcement action; after that, civil penalty up to $7,500 per violation, plus possible injunction and recovery of attorney fees/investigative expenses (§ 30-14-2820).

items.title: Nebraska Financial Data Protection and Consumer Notification of Data Security Breach Act
items.applies_to_vendor: § 87-803: a data processor/third party that maintains but does not own personal information must 'give notice to and cooperate with the owner or licensee' upon discovering a breach. § 87-808 separately requires any entity disclosing personal data to an unaffiliated third-party service provider to contractually require that provider to implement reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the type of information disclosed.
key_obligations: Entities owning/licensing personal data must notify affected Nebraska residents when a breach occurs and unauthorized acquisition/use is reasonably believed likely (§ 87-803).
Data processors/third parties maintaining data they do not own must notify and cooperate with the owner/licensee upon discovering a breach (§ 87-803).
Notice to residents must be made as soon as possible and without unreasonable delay (§ 87-803).
Notice to the Nebraska Attorney General must be provided no later than the time notice is provided to the first Nebraska resident (§ 87-803).

Any entity disclosing personal data to a third-party service provider must contractually require that provider to implement reasonable security procedures and practices, tailored to the data type; this applies to service-provider contracts renewed on or after July 19, 2018 (§ 87-808).
items.notice_deadline: "as soon as possible and without unreasonable delay"; AG notice "not later than the time when notice is provided to the Nebraska resident."
items.regulator_notice: Attorney General must be notified no later than resident notice; AG may issue subpoenas and seek direct economic damages for affected residents.
items.penalties: A violation of § 87-808 (security-procedures/contract-flowdown requirement) is treated as a violation of the Nebraska Consumer Protection Act (§ 59-1602) — an unfair or deceptive trade practice — enforced exclusively by the Attorney General; no private right of action.
items.effective_or_amended: § 87-808 contract-flowdown requirement effective for contracts entered into or renewed on or after July 19, 2018.

items.title: Nevada school service provider — pupil data privacy
items.applies_to_vendor: Directly regulates a "school service provider" (defined at NRS 388.284) providing a "school service" (NRS 388.283) that involves personally identifiable information (NRS 388.282) of Nevada pupils.
key_obligations: School service provider must provide written disclosure to certain persons/entities and notice of changes to its data-security plan; must allow review/correction of personally identifiable information (NRS 388.291).

Collection and use of personally identifiable information by a school service provider is limited; the provider may not engage in targeted advertising to pupils based on such information, and may not use it to amass a profile about a pupil except in furtherance of the school service for which it was disclosed (NRS 388.292).
Transfer or disclosure of personally identifiable information to third parties is restricted, with redaction available on request; NRS 388.292 also states a penalty for violation.
Provider must maintain a data-security plan and give notice of security breaches; successor entities of school service providers are addressed (NRS 388.293).
Waiver or modification of any right, obligation, or liability under these provisions is prohibited (NRS 388.296).
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Defined terms include "personally identifiable information" (388.282), "school service" (388.283), "school service provider" (388.284), and "targeted advertising" (388.285).
items.penalties: NRS 388.292's heading states it includes a "penalty for violation of provisions"; the specific penalty amount/mechanism was not retrieved from the fetched excerpt this session.

items.title: Nevada online privacy notice / sale of covered information — NOT a comprehensive controller/processor privacy law
items.applies_to_vendor: Applies to "operators" (entities that own/operate an internet website or online service for commercial purposes, collect/maintain covered information from Nevada residents who use/visit the site, and process that information) and "data brokers." This is materially narrower than a VCDPA/CCPA-style comprehensive law: it does not create a general controller/processor framework, data-protection-assessment requirement, or broad consumer rights (access/correct/portability) — it is limited to a privacy-notice requirement and a right to opt out of the *sale* of covered information to a third party for that third party to license or sell further.
key_obligations: Operator must provide a privacy notice identifying categories of covered information collected and third-party sharing practices (NRS 603A.340).
Nevada residents may submit a verified request directing an operator not to sell their covered information (NRS 603A.345); a similar opt-out mechanism applies to data brokers (NRS 603A.346).
Operator/data broker must respond to a verified opt-out request within 60 days, extendable by 30 days.

Does NOT establish rights to access, correct, delete, or port personal data, and does NOT impose controller/processor contractual-flowdown obligations comparable to Virginia/Colorado/Montana-style comprehensive privacy acts.
items.notice_deadline: 60-day response period for verified opt-out requests, extendable by 30 days.
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Covered information" is defined narrowly around internet-collected identifiers/categories tied to the operator's website or online service, not the broader "personal data" definition used in comprehensive state privacy acts.
items.penalties: Attorney General enforces; civil penalty up to $5,000 per violation, sought in district court (NRS 603A.360(2)-(3)). No private right of action identified.
